7, 13, 14, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 28, July 16, 19, 24, 2007

RULING RESPECTING PRIVILEGED COMMUNICATIONS – POLICE
IMPERSONATING
ALLEGED RELIGIOUS ADVISOR

O’CONNOR J.

[
1
]

The Applicants, Evol Robinson and Reuben
Pinnock, together with Jahmar Welsh are charged with the first degree murder of
Youhan Oraha, who was shot to death in Brampton on October 9, 2004.

[
2
]

During their investigation of the murder, the
police deployed an undercover officer, Constable Andrew Cooper, who played the
role of a spiritual advisor known as an
Obeah
or
Obeahman
.   He called
himself ‘Leon’.  Among some cultures in the Caribbean
Islands, an
Obeahman
is believed to have the
ability to communicate with the spirit world and to influence events and people
in the physical world.    Some of the Applicants’ family members were born and
raised in Jamaica.  The
officer, also from Jamaica and
familiar with the practice of
Obeah
, introduced himself into the Applicants’
social circle by befriending Collet Robinson, the mother of Evol Robinson and
Jahmar Welsh.  He met numerous times with her and Messrs. Robinson and Pinnock,
convincingly playing his role by conversing with them partly in Jamaican patois
and by reciting the incantations and displaying the symbols and paraphernalia
of
Obeah
.  He told them they had to confide to him what they knew about the
death of the Youhan Oraha.  He elicited inculpatory statements from Messrs.
Robinson and Pinnock as well as investigatively helpful information from Collet
Robinson by convincing them he had the power to protect them from the evil
spirit of Mr. Oraha.  Leon also
told them he had the power to cause the police and members of the judiciary to
become ill, thus protecting them from prosecution for criminal offences.

[
3
]

All of the meetings were audio recorded and most
were also video taped.  The Crown seeks to introduce into evidence at the trial
the utterances of the participants in the
Obeah
sessions.

[
4
]

The two Applicants seek orders excluding the
evidence on several grounds that engage both the
Charter
and the common
law.  The issues to be explored are:

(a)

whether the police tactics constituted an infringement
of their s.2(a)
Charter
rights to freedom of religion;

(b)

whether the police tactics constituted a “dirty
trick” that would shock the conscience of the community and would bring the
administration of justice into disrepute;

(c)

whether the Applicants’ s.15
Charter

rights were breached.  They argue they were discriminated against by the police
who employed the
Obeah
sting only because they are black people of Caribbean origin;

(d)

whether the police conduct violated their common
law right to protection of religious communication.

Background

Defining Religion/Religious Belief System

[
5
]

Determining whether
Obeah
or any other
belief system should be accorded protection, under the
Charter
or common
law, is an undertaking that must consider the acute sensitivities attached to
religious beliefs and practices, particularly in a multicultural context.  In
considering the issues raised in this case - the nature of religion, in general,
the status of
Obeah
, in particular - and the constitutional guarantees
for freedom of conscience, religion and thought – a Court must be ever-mindful
of the multicultural precepts and principles upon which Canadian society is
predicated.

[
6
]

Canada, as a pluralistic
nation, is widely celebrated for the diversity of beliefs and practices that
comprise the country’s multicultural mosaic.
This vision of Canadian society is
eloquently expressed in the words of the majority in
R. v. Big M Drug Mart
Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
[1985]
1 S.C.R. 295
at 330,
a case that explored the parameters of s.2 (a) of the
Charter
:

A truly free society is one which can accommodate a
wide variety of beliefs, diversity of tastes and pursuits, customs and codes of
conduct.  A free society is one which aims at equality with respect to the
enjoyment of fundamental freedoms . . .

These abiding
values of tolerance and acceptance are further enshrined in s.27 of the
Charter

as follows:

This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner
consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage
of Canadians.

[
7
]

While Canadian courts are often called upon to
adjudicate matters involving religious groups and competing rights, it is not
the Courts’ role to make substantive pronouncements upon religions and their
adherents.  To do so would involve an unacceptable degree of subjective
reasoning and analysis on the part of the judiciary, inevitably leading to
unfortunate and questionable results.

[
8
]

In
Syndicat Northcrest v.
Amselem
,
2004 SCC 47 (CanLII)
,
[2004] S.C.J. No. 46
,
at para.
50
, Iacobucci
J. said:

In my view, the State is in no position to be,
nor should it become, the arbiter of religious dogma. Accordingly, courts
should avoid judicially interpreting and thus determining, either explicitly or
implicitly, the content of a subjective understanding of religious requirement,
“obligation”, precept, “commandment”, custom or ritual.  Secular judicial determinations
of theological or religious disputes, or of contentious matters of religious
doctrine, unjustifiably entangle the court in the affairs of religion.

[
9
]

T
his sentiment is echoed by the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Church of Scientology and The Queen
(No.6),

Re

(1987), 31 C.C.C. (3d) 449 at p. 481
citing with approval the words
of the Australian High Court in
Church of New Faith v. Commissioner of
Pay-Roll Tax

(1983), 154 C.L.R. 120 (H.C. of Australia) at 150
:

The truth or falsity of religions is not the business of
officials or the courts. If
each purported
religion had to show that its doctrines were true, then all
might fail. Administrators and judges must resist
the temptation to hold that
groups or
institutions are not religious because claimed religious beliefs or
practices
seem
absurd, fraudulent, evil or novel
; or because the group or
insti­
tution is new, the number of adherents
small, the leaders hypocrites, or
because
they seek to obtain the financial and other privileges which come with
religious status. In the eyes of the law,
religions are equal. There is no
religious
club with a monopoly of State privileges for its members. The policy
of
the law is "one in, all in". (emphasis added)

[
10
]

T
hus, it is not the
task of this Court to determine whether or not
Obeah
is a religion
worthy of mainstream recognition; rather, it is necessary only to determine
whether the constellation of beliefs and practices for which
Obeah
is
traditionally known are such that they merit consideration under s.2(a) of the
Charter

and under the common law privilege for religious communication.

[
11
]

The Applicants called the opinion evidence of four academics, all of
whom were qualified as experts in fields related to religious history and
experience.  They offered scholarly insights into the challenges inherent in categorizing
and quantifying religion and religious belief systems.  The experts included
Dr. Abraham Khan, a professor of divinity at the University of Toronto’s Trinity College, Dr. Frances Henry, a social anthropologist and a professor
emeritus

at York University, Dr. Kamari
Clarke, an associate professor of political anthropology at Yale University and Dr. James Beverley, a professor of
Christian thought and ethics at Tyndale Seminary in Toronto.  All of the experts were united in the view that religious beliefs
are broad and varied and often defy precise measurement.

•

Dr. Khan said that “…There are many different
belief systems or perceptions of reality within the area of religion.”  (page 2
of his report)

•

Dr. Henry said that “…It is difficult to define
‘religion’.  Not only are there many definitions available in the literature
but the entire area of human belief and practice formerly subsumed under the
rubric ‘religion’ is increasingly being problematized by scholars and theorists
of ‘religious’ behaviour.  Older definitions are being challenged because there
are so many new forms of religious behaviour found in the increasingly
globalized world.” (page 1 of her report)

•

Dr. Clarke notes at page 2 of her report that “…
world religions are not static entities.  They have been recognized by
academics, theologians, and practitioners alike to be fluid – evolving over
time, along with the cultures within which they are expressed – and their
adherents continue to use these religions to adapt to change and to make
meaning of life.” And at page 2 she says that “…Religion, broadly defined,
represents a sphere of cultural meanings, practices, beliefs, and forms of
social logics that enables people to understand their social world.”

•

Dr. Beverley offered that “…Religious scholars have
increasingly recognized the danger of according privileged religious status to
religions simply because they are mainstream and established.” (page 2 of his
report)

[
12
]

The experts were also united in the view that the dominant
Judeo-Christian construct may not necessarily serve as an appropriate or
relevant comparative standard, particularly when dealing with lesser-known or
less widely practiced belief systems.  All were firmly of the view that
Obeah

met the criteria of a religious belief system.  Dr. Henry said that “…
Obeah

is therefore part of a larger and more multifaceted ‘religious’ system.”  Dr.
Clark explored the incantations and rituals carried out by the undercover police

Obeahman
and said that “…The practices performed by Leon appear to represent a form of ritual
practice that appears to be
Obeah
and is quite similar to that of
Santeria

as well as other syncretized forms of religious practices.” (page 5 of her
report)

[
13
]

Thus, it is within this nebulous philosophical zone that
Obeah

resides – not immediately recognizable as a religion according to the dominant
religious paradigms, yet accepted by those who identify themselves as adherents
and practitioners and recognized as such by experts in various fields of
religious studies.

The Rowe Case

[
14
]

In
R. v. Rowe
(2006),
2006 CanLII 14235 (ON CA)
, 208 C.C.C. (3d) 412 (O.C.A.), the Court
upheld the ruling of Thomas J., the trial judge, who had admitted the
statements of Rowe to an
Obeahman
after he had murdered a bank employee
during an armed robbery.  The Crown attorney and some of the investigating
officers in
Rowe
are involved in the case at bar.  The use by the police
of the
Obeah
sting in this case was prompted and informed by their experience
and success in
Rowe
.  In his written submissions on this application,
the Crown argues that “…the legal issues in this Application are identical to
those in
Rowe
”.

[
15
]

Although there are similarities between the two cases – both involved
the status of
Obeah
as religion or a religious belief system – the
differences are sufficiently compelling to require a fresh analysis of the
legal issues.

[
16
]

Following are some of the factual differences between this case and
Rowe
:

•

In
Rowe
, the police did not initiate the
communication between the spiritual advisor and the accused parties; the
relationship was pre-existing.  In this case, the police created the relationship
and initiated and staged all aspects of the communication.

•

In
Rowe
, the meetings were entirely secular
in nature.  In this case, the police had to be aware that religious rights of
the defendants were engaged.  In support of this position, the Applicants point
to the involvement of Det. Sgt. Jarvis in both matters as well as his exposure
at the
Rowe
trial to the testimony of Professor Henry regarding the
status of
Obeah
as involving a system of religious beliefs.

•

In
Rowe
, there was a tangible and
pre-existing connection between the
Obeah
/Rowe relationship and the
crime being investigated.  In this case, no such connection existed.

•

In
Rowe
, police involvement in the relationship
between the
Obeahman
and Rowe did not cause a breach of trust as there
was no evidence, direct or circumstantial, that Rowe believed in any “powers”
that the
Obeahman
may have had (see the OCA judgment at paragraphs
57-59).  In this case, the investigative methods chosen by police involved an
inevitable and serious breach of trust.

[
17
]

Other factual differences include:

•

Collet and, to a lesser extent, Evol Robinson
believed in Leon’s spiritual powers
as an
Obeah
practitioner.

•

The Applicants never asked the
Obeahman
,
Leon, to use his powers for a specific purpose nor did they have any specific
targets or goals.  Leon was never
asked to physically or psychologically harm an identified target.  He was never
asked to commit a physical act in the concrete world.  He promoted or suggested
to them that he could harm the police and the judiciary.  He told them he had
the “power” to protect them from the “Beast man” and the “Babylon System”,
Obeah

terms for the police, the courts and the authorities.  The Applicants, in turn,
did not reject this suggestion as wrong, but appeared to acquiesce with the
suggestions made.  Thus, it is clear that the “corruption/unlawful purpose” in
their relationship with Leon was
manufactured by the police.

The Alleged Violation of S.2(a) of the
Charter

Section 2(a) of
the Charter reads:

Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(
a)
freedom
of conscience and religion;

[
18
]

In
Big M Drug Mart Ltd
., when examining the nature of the
s.2(a)
Charter
right to freedom of religion, Dickson J. framed the issue
in terms of whether the police conduct interfered with the Applicants’ ability
to worship freely or to practice in accordance with their religious beliefs.
At paragraphs 94 and 95 he said:

The essence of the concept of freedom of religion
is the right to entertain such religious beliefs as a person chooses, the right
to declare religious beliefs openly and without fear of hindrance or reprisal,
and the right to manifest religious belief by worship and practice or by
teaching and dissemination. But the concept means more than that.

Freedom can primarily
be characterized by the absence of coercion or constraint. If a person is
compelled by the state or the will of another to a course of action or inaction
which he would not otherwise have chosen, he is not acting of his own volition
and he cannot be said to be truly free. One of the major purposes of the
Charter

is to protect, within reason, from compulsion or restraint. Coercion includes
not only such blatant forms of compulsion as direct commands to act or refrain
from acting on pain of sanction, coercion includes indirect forms of control
which determine or limit alternative courses of conduct available to others. Freedom
in a broad sense embraces both the absence of coercion and constraint, and the
right to manifest beliefs and practices. Freedom means that, subject to such
limitations as are necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals
or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others, no one is to be forced to act
in a way contrary to his beliefs or his conscience.

[
19
]

In
R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R. 713
,
Dickson C.J. said at paragraphs 96 and 97:

It matters not, I believe, whether a coercive
burden is direct or indirect, intentional or unintentional, foreseeable or
unforeseeable. All coercive burdens on the exercise of religious beliefs are
potentially within the ambit of s.2(a).

This does not mean, however, that every burden on
religious practices is offensive to the constitutional guarantee of freedom of
religion. It means only that indirect or unintentional burdens will not be held
to be outside the scope of
Charter
protection on that account alone.
Section 2(
a
) does not require the legislatures to eliminate every
miniscule state‑imposed cost associated with the practice of religion.
Otherwise the
Charter
would offer protection from innocuous secular
legislation such as a taxation act that imposed a modest sales tax extending to
all products, including those used in the course of religious worship. In my
opinion, it is unnecessary to turn to s.1 in order to justify legislation of
that sort. The purpose of s.2(
a
) is to ensure that society does not
interfere with profoundly personal beliefs that govern one's perception of
oneself, humankind, nature, and, in some cases, a higher or different order of
being. These beliefs, in turn, govern one's conduct and practices. The
Constitution shelters individuals and groups only to the extent that religious
beliefs or conduct might reasonably or actually be threatened. For a state‑imposed
cost or burden to be proscribed by s.2(
a
) it must be capable of
interfering with religious belief or practice. In short, legislative or
administrative action which increases the cost of practising or otherwise
manifesting religious beliefs
is not prohibited if
the burden is trivial or insubstantial: see, on this point,
R. v. Jones
,

1986 CanLII 32 (S.C.C.)
,
[
1986] 2 S.C.R.
284,
per
Wilson J. at p. 314.

[
20
]

In
Syndicat
, Iacobucci J. made it
clear that the freedom is not limitless.  He said at paragraph 62:

Freedom of religion, as outlined above, quite
appropriately reflects a broad and expansive approach to religious freedom
under both  the Quebec
Charter
and the
Canadian
Charter
and should not be
prematurely narrowly construed. However, our jurisprudence does not allow
individuals to do absolutely anything in the name of that freedom. Even if
individuals demonstrate that they sincerely believe in the religious essence of
an action, for example, that a particular practice will subjectively engender a
genuine connection with the divine or with the subject or object of their
faith, and even if they successfully demonstrate non-trivial or
non-insubstantial interference with that practice, they will still have to
consider how the exercise of  their right impacts upon the rights of
others in the context of the competing rights of private individuals. Conduct
which would potentially cause harm to or interference with the rights of others
would not automatically be protected. The ultimate protection of any particular

Charter
right must be measured in relation to other rights and with a
view to the underlying context in which the apparent conflict arises.

[
21
]

In
Multani v. Commission Scolaire
Marguerite-Bourgeoys,
2006 SCC 6 (CanLII)
,
[2006] S.C.J. No. 6

Charron J. said at paragraph 30:

This Court has frequently stated, and rightly
so, that freedom of religion is not absolute and that it can conflict with
other constitutional rights…

[
22
]

In
British Columbia College of Teachers v.
Trinity Western University

et al
,
2001 SCC 31 (CanLII)
,
[2001] 1 S.C.R. 772
at para.

30
, Iacobucci & Bastarache JJ. said:

Similarly, Iacobucci and Major JJ.
concluded in B. (R.) v. Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto,
B. (R.) v. Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan
Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 115 (SCC)
,
[1995] 1 S.C.R. 315

,
at para.
226
, that:

Just as there are limits to the ambit of freedom of
expression (e.g. s.2(b) does not protect violent acts: R. v. Zundel,
1992 CanLII 75 (SCC)
,
[1992] 2 S.C.R. 731
, at pp. 753 and 801
; R. v.
Keegstra,
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
,
[1990] 3 S.C.R. 697
, at pp. 732 and 830)
, so are
there limits to the scope of s.2(a), especially so when this provision is
called upon to protect
activity that threatens the physical or psychological
well-being of others.
In other words, although the freedom of belief may be
broad, the freedom to act upon those beliefs is considerably narrower, and it
is the latter freedom at issue in this case. [Emphasis added.]

[
23
]

In
Ross v.
New Brunswick
School District No. 15
,
1996 CanLII 237 (SCC)
, [1996] S.C.J. No. 40,
LaForest J. said
at paragraph 72:

Indeed, this
Court has affirmed that freedom of  religion ensures that every individual must
be free to hold and to manifest without State interference those beliefs and
opinions dictated by one's conscience. This freedom is not unlimited, however,
and is restricted by the right of others to hold and to manifest beliefs and
opinions of their own, and to be free from injury from the exercise of the
freedom of religion of others. Freedom of religion is subject to such
limitations as are necessary to protect public safety, order, health or morals
and the fundamental rights and freedoms of others.

[
24
]

Thus, the question to be engaged and analyzed is whether the Applicants
were restricted in their religious practice or coerced directly or indirectly
by the police conduct, to do something they would otherwise have not done or
not do something they would otherwise have done
in respect of or related to
their religious beliefs
.  The Applicants profess to be practitioners of
Obeah
.
To engage
s.2(a)

Charter
protection, they must demonstrate that their
right to practice
Obeah
was interfered with or restricted by the undercover
police officer/
Obeahman
or that they were coerced into conduct that had
the result of preventing them from practicing their particular religious belief
system.  To demonstrate merely that they were coerced or berated or even
threatened by the
Obeahman
into confessing to a crime would not attract
s.2(a) protection, as such conduct would not have interfered with their right
to practice their form of religion.  As the Supreme Court said in
Edwards
Books
, at paragraph 97, “For a state-imposed cost or burden to be
proscribed by s.2(a) it must be capable of interfering with religious belief or
practice.”  And further, even if the Applicants demonstrate the police conduct
did amount to such an interference or coercion
qua
their religious
practices, they must show that it was more than a trivial or insubstantial
interference.

[
25
]

The Applicants submit that their rights under
s.2(a) were infringed by the police undercover investigation.  They argue they
meet the two-part test in
Syndicat,
set out at paragraph 56:

Thus, at the first stage of a religious freedom
analysis, an individual advancing an issue premised upon a freedom of religion
claim must show the court that  (1) he or she has a practice or
belief, having a nexus with religion, which calls for a particular line of
conduct, either by being objectively or subjectively obligatory or customary,
or by, in general, subjectively engendering a personal connection with the
divine or with the subject or object of an individual's spiritual faith,
irrespective of whether a particular practice or belief is required by official
religious dogma or is in conformity with the position of religious officials;
and (2) he or she is sincere in his or her belief. Only then will freedom of
religion be triggered.

[
26
]

The court in
Syndicat,
at paragraph 39, adopts the following
characterization of “religion”:

In order to define religious
freedom, we must first ask ourselves what we mean by "religion".
While it is perhaps not possible to define religion precisely, some outer
definition is useful since only beliefs, convictions and practices rooted in
religion, as opposed to those that are secular, socially based or
conscientiously held, are protected by the guarantee of freedom of religion. Defined
broadly, religion typically involves a particular and comprehensive system of
faith and worship. Religion also tends to involve the belief in a divine,
superhuman or controlling power. In essence, religion is

about freely and deeply held personal convictions or beliefs
connected to an individual's spiritual faith and integrally linked to one's
self-definition and spiritual fulfilment, the practices of which allow
individuals to foster a connection with the divine or with the subject or
object of that spiritual faith.

[
27
]

F
urther, at para. 42, Iacobucci J. speaks
of “
a personal or subjective conception of freedom of religion, one
that is integrally linked with an individual's self-definition and fulfilment
and is a function of personal autonomy and choice, elements which
undergird the right”.  At paragraph 43, Iacobucci J. said:

The emphasis then is on personal choice of
religious beliefs. In my opinion, these decisions and commentary should not be
construed to imply that freedom of religion protects only those aspects of
religious belief or conduct that are objectively recognized by religious
experts as being obligatory tenets or precepts of a particular religion.
Consequently, claimants seeking to invoke freedom of religion should not need
to prove the objective validity of their beliefs in that their beliefs are
objectively recognized as valid by other members of the same religion, nor is
such an inquiry appropriate for courts to make; see, e.g.,
Re Funk and
Manitoba Labour Board
(1976),
1976 CanLII 1098 (MB CA)
,
66 D.L.R. (3d) 35

(Man. C.A.), at pp.
37-38. In fact, this Court has indicated on several occasions that, if
anything, a person must show "[s]incerity of belief" (
Edwards
Books, supra
, at p. 735) and not that a particular belief is
"valid".

[
28
]

Like the experts in this case, the Supreme Court rejects a narrow,
overly-precise definition of religion in favour of a broad perspective that
could conceivably capture an array of beliefs that, like
Obeah
, fall
outside of well-recognized religious boundaries.

[
29
]

In this case, the evidence of the four experts, particularly Drs.
Henry and Clarke, clearly and convincingly establish that
Obeah
is a religious
belief system that meets the Supreme Court definition of such in
Syndicat

and thus warrants s.2(a) protection.  The Crown did not call any experts to
contradict the Applicants’ evidence, but instead relied on cross-examination of
the experts and on the opinion of Det. Sgt. Jarvis that
Obeah
was not a
religion or a religious belief system.  The experts were not shaken or
contradicted in their opinions.  Det. Sgt. Jarvis is not an expert in religious
belief systems.    The Applicants have met the first stage of the
Syndicat

test.

[
30
]

At the second stage of the analysis, the Applicants must show that their
belief is sincerely held.  If a claimant lacks sincerity in his or her alleged
beliefs, then the
Charter
protection under s.2(a) will not be triggered.

[
31
]

On the Court’s ability to determine the sincerity of a party’s
belief, Iacobucci J. in
Syndicat
states at para. 51:

…while a court is not qualified to rule on the
validity or veracity of any given religious practice or belief, or to choose
among various interpretations of belief, it is qualified to inquire into the
sincerity of a claimant's belief, where sincerity is in fact at issue: see
Jones
,
supra
;
Ross, supra
. It is important to emphasize, however, that
sincerity of belief simply implies an honesty of belief: see
Thomas v.
Review Board of the
Indiana
Employment Security Division, supra
.

[
32
]

The Court’s assessment of a claimant’s sincerity is a question of
fact that must be as limited as possible.  The purpose of the sincerity inquiry
is only to ensure that the “presently asserted religious belief is in good
faith, neither fictitious nor capricious, and that it is not an artifice.
Otherwise, nothing short of a religious inquisition would be required to
decipher the innermost beliefs of human beings”. (para. 52)

[
33
]

The court provides a non-exhaustive list of criteria to be employed
in the sincerity analysis, including the credibility of a claimant's testimony,
as well as an analysis of whether the alleged belief is consistent with his or
her other current religious practices.

[
34
]

Iacobucci J., however, cautions courts against rigourously studying
and focusing on the past practices of claimants in order to determine whether
their current beliefs are sincerely held.  At para. 53, he states, “Because of
the vacillating nature of religious belief, a court's inquiry into sincerity,
if anything, should focus not on past practice or past belief but on a person's
belief at the time of the alleged interference with his or her religious
freedom”.

[
35
]

With respect to a claimants’ onus, he says at paragraph 54:

A claimant may choose to adduce expert evidence
to demonstrate that his or her belief is consistent with the practices and
beliefs of other adherents of the faith. While such evidence may be relevant
to a demonstration of sincerity, it is not necessary. Since the focus of
the inquiry is not on what others view the claimant's religious obligations as
being, but rather what the claimant views these
personal   religious "obligations" to be, it is
inappropriate to require expert opinions to show sincerity of belief. An
"expert" or an authority on religious law is not the surrogate for an
individual's affirmation of what his or her religious beliefs are. Religious
belief is intensely personal and can easily vary from one individual to
another. Requiring proof of the established practices of a religion to gauge
the sincerity of belief diminishes the very freedom we seek to protect.

[
36
]

The Applicants did not testify as to the sincerity of their beliefs
in
Obeah
.  The video/audio-taped sessions involving them and Const.
Cooper are the only instructive evidence on this issue.  Although some of the
experts opined that Robinson appeared sincere in his acceptance of the rituals
and incantations of Leon, these
views have no evidentiary value, as
Syndicat
holds that “…it is
inappropriate to require expert opinions to show sincerity of belief.  An
“expert” or an authority on religious law is not the surrogate for an
individual’s affirmation of what his or her religious beliefs are…”

37
]

While this Applicant dutifully attended at the sessions with Leon, he was there only because the
arrangements had been made by Collet Robinson on his behalf and she had
instructed him to attend.  When there he displayed either a distinct lack of
interest in the process or considerable scepticism of what Leon was saying.  He often failed to
respond to questions and comments from Leon or did so with short, sometimes incoherent answers.  He never
directly answered Leon’s persistent prodding about his belief in his (Leon’s) powers and in
Obeah
.

[
39
]

Based on this evidence, I cannot conclude that Mr. Pinnock’s
asserted religious belief is sincerely held.  His attendance at the sessions
was primarily to mollify Collet Robinson and probably to satisfy his own curiosity.
But there is simply insufficient evidence that he held a good faith belief in
the process.  Thus, he has failed to demonstrate that his
s.2(a)

Charter

rights to freedom of religion have been engaged.

[
40
]

As to the Applicant Evol Robinson, his conduct and his demeanour
during his communications with Leon demonstrate that his belief in
Obeah
was sincerely held at
the time of those communications. He professed genuine belief in the power of
Obeah

and repeatedly affirmed his belief.  His admissions to Leon directly resulted from those convictions.  Thus, his
s.2(a)

Charter

rights have been triggered.

[
41
]

Thus, at the next stage of the
Syndicat
analysis it is
necessary to consider the degree of the interference with the exercise of Mr.
Robinson’s religious freedom.  He must show that the impugned government
conduct interfered with his ability to act in accordance with his religious
practices or beliefs in a manner that is more than trivial or insubstantial.  Even
where a claimant demonstrates that the degree of interference constitutes a
Charter

infringement, it is still open to the Courts to conduct a competing rights
analysis and find that the impugned religious action is unworthy of protection
if the implicated conduct could conceivably cause harm or affect the rights of
others.  As Iacobucci J. said at paragraph 63 of
Syndicat
, “…it should be
emphasized that not every action will become summarily unassailable and receive
automatic protection under the banner of freedom of religion. No right,
including freedom of religion, is absolute.”  And in
Children’s Aid Society
of Metropolitan Toronto
,
the Supreme Court said at paragraph 30 that “…Just
as there are limits to the ambit of freedom of expression (e.g. s.2(b) does not
protect violent acts)…so there are limits to the scope of s.2(a), especially so
when this provision is called upon to protect activity that threatens the
physical or psychological well-being of others…”

[
42
]

Thus, this Applicant must demonstrate that the degree of
interference with his religious freedom was more than trivial or insubstantial
and if so, that it would not threaten or cause physical or psychological harm
to the well-being of others.  In my view, he has not succeeded on the first point.
While the police conduct did interfere to a degree with his religious freedom,
it did not do so in a manner that was more than trivial or insubstantial.  He
was not constrained or coerced in his religious practice. The planted fake religious
leader did not interfere with his freedom to worship or express himself
spiritually.  In fact, Leon
encouraged him to believe in
Obeah
, to participate in the chanting, the
use of candles and handkerchiefs and the various rituals of the belief system,
as only then could he help him defeat those who wished to harm him.  While Leon was a fake, playing on the Applicant’s
belief in his authority as a spiritual leader who could bring him positive
benefits, i.e. protection from evil spirits and from prosecution, Leon did
nothing to interfere with this Applicant’s ability or right to worship, nor did
he coerce him to disbelieve or disavow his religious beliefs.

[
43
]

The question of whether the religious activity would have impinged
the rights of others by causing them harm need not be explored.   If, however,
the analysis had reached that point, I would have found that the harm
contemplated, even though real in the mind of the Applicant, would have been
protected by s.2(a).  The harm, if any, being implored of the deity was one
sought through a spiritual route.  To seek the intervention of a divine being,
to cause harm to others, even death to one’s enemies, or to acquire any other
secular end, such as success in sports or business, is not wrong.  Most
religions encourage some form of communication with a deity to achieve such goals.
It is called praying.  What is wrong, as was the case in
Rowe
, is the
seeking of harm to others through secular, rather than spiritual means.  The
Obeahman

in
Rowe
encouraged the accused to commit bank robberies.  Seeking a
result from one’s deity is a protected religious experience, while seeking a
result through secular means is not protected.  In
Church of Scientology
,
the Ontario Court of Appeal approved the Australian High Court in
Church of
New Faith
when it found that courts must recognize all religions even when
their “…religious beliefs or practices seem absurd, fraudulent,
evil
or
novel…” (emphasis added).

Section 1 – Reasonable Limits
Analysis

[
44
]

Even if this Court had found that Mr. Robinson’s

s.2 (a)

Charter
right was infringed by the conduct of the police
investigation, I would have found that the impugned police conduct can be
justified as a “reasonable limit” under
s.1
of the
Charter
on the
Applicant’s freedom of religion.

[
45
]

Section 1 reads:

The
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it
subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably
justified in a free and democratic society.

[
46
]

In such an analysis the onus is on the Crown, as the party seeking
to uphold the constitutionality of the limitation, to meet the reasonable
limits test.

[
47
]

It is important to note the novel nature of Applicant Robinson’s
constitutional argument.  The remedy he is seeking for the alleged breach of
his
s.2(a)

Charter
rights is the exclusion of evidence at his trial, not
the restoration of a lost or interfered with religious right, the usual result
sought in the cases on this issue.  A
s.1
analysis will not resolve the
evidentiary status of the communications. Section 1 can only address the
constitutionality of the police conduct.

[
48
]

Nevertheless, if the Applicant had proven that his freedom of
religion has been breached by the police investigation, the impugned
investigative tactic would be subjected to s.1 scrutiny.  Charron J., in
Multan,

makes it clear that s.2(a) competing rights and infringement claims
are to be addressed under s.1:

This Court has clearly recognized that freedom
of religion can be limited when a person's freedom to act in accordance with
his or her beliefs may cause harm to or interfere with the rights of others
(see
R. v. Big M Drug Mart
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R. 295
,
at p. 337, and
Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem
,
[2004] 2 S.C.R. 551
,

2004 SCC 47
, at
para.
62
). However, the Court has on numerous occasions stressed the advantages
of reconciling competing rights by means of a s.1 analysis. For example, in
B.
(R.) v. Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 115 (SCC)
,
[1995] 1 S.C.R. 315
,
the claimants, who were Jehovah's Witnesses, contested an order that authorized
the administration of a blood transfusion to their daughter. While
acknowledging that freedom of religion could be limited in the best interests
of the child, La Forest J., writing for the majority of the Court, stated the
following, at paras. 109-10:

This Court has consistently
refrained from formulating internal limits to the scope of freedom of religion
in cases where the constitutionality of a legislative scheme was raised; it
rather opted to balance the competing rights under
s.1
of the
Charter
...

In my view, it appears sounder to
leave to the state the burden of justifying the restrictions it has chosen. Any
ambiguity or hesitation should be resolved in favour of individual rights. Not
only is this consistent with the broad and liberal interpretation of rights
favoured by this Court, but s.1 is a much more flexible tool with which to
balance competing rights than s.2(
a
).

The Oakes Test

[
49
]

The s.1 test for “reasonable limits” was
established in
R. v. Oakes
,

1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
,
[1986] 1 S.C.R. 103
,
and involves an inquiry into the importance of the objective of a
limiting measure, and the reasonableness of the means adopted to achieve the
objective.

[
50
]

At the first stage, the party seeking to uphold the limitation must
establish the importance of the legislative objective.  At the second stage,
the Court will consider the reasonableness of the means adopted to achieve that
objective by way of a three-part assessment of the proportionality of the means
used to the ends achieved.

[
51
]

The legislative objective, which the measures
responsible for a limit are designed to serve, must be of sufficient importance
to warrant overriding a constitutionally protected right or freedom.  The
standard must be high in order to ensure that objectives which are trivial or
discordant with the principles integral to a free and democratic society do not
gain s.1 protection.  At a minimum, an objective must relate to concerns
which are pressing and substantial before it can be characterized as
sufficiently important.

[
52
]

The party invoking s.1 must then show that the
means chosen are reasonable and demonstrably justified, which involves of
proportionality test having three elements:

(
a) the measures adopted must be carefully
designed to achieve the objective in question.  They must not be
arbitrary, unfair or based on irrational considerations;

(b) the
means, even if rationally connected to the objective in the first sense, should
impair as little as possible the right or freedom in question; and

(c)
there must be a proportionality between the effects of the measures and the
objective which has been identified as one of sufficient importance.
[1]

Applying
the Test

[
53
]

The Crown must first demonstrate that the objective of the impugned
police conduct is sufficiently pressing and substantial.

[
54
]

The starting point for analyzing the importance
of the challenged conduct is a consideration of the broader societal context in
which the conduct occurs.  In the words of Bastarache J. in
Thomson

Newspapers v.
Canada
(Attorney
General),

1998 CanLII 829 (SCC)
,
[1998] 1
S.C.R. 877
.at para.
87:

The analysis under
s.1
of the
Charter

must be undertaken with a close attention to context.  This is inevitable
as the test devised
in
R. v. Oakes
,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
,
[1986] 1 S.C.R. 103
, requires a
court to establish the objective of the impugned provision, which can only be
accomplished by canvassing the nature of the social problem which it
addresses.

[
55
]

Violent crime in Canadian
society, particularly where guns are involved, is one of the most pressing
social concerns of our day. At p. 20 of the “Respondent Crown’s Additional
Argument – Rowe Application,” the Crown submits that “…Solving firearm
homicides is and has been a subject of great societal angst in the Greater
Toronto Area in recent years.”

[
56
]

Firearms-related violence in the city of Toronto has become so prevalent that 2005 became
known as the “Year of the Gun”.  During the second week in May of 2007 alone, t
here were nine reported shooting incidents. (The

Toronto
Star, May 25, 2007.)

[
57
]

In
R. v. Grant
,

2006 CanLII 18347 (ON CA)
,
[2006] O.J. No. 2179
, at para.
66
, Laskin J.A. said, “. . .
increasing levels of gun violence in our communities threaten
everyone's personal freedom”.

[
58
]

The police man the front lines of the war
against this form of violence.  Their investigation of criminal activity,
including undercover operations, are an essential and unavoidable feature of
contemporary crime prevention programs and strategies.  In
Regina
v. Roberts
,
1997 CanLII 3313 (BC CA)
,
[1997] B.C.J. No. 765
(B.C.C.A.)
at para.
13
the
Court adopted the position of
the
Manitoba
Court
of Appeal in
R. v. Unger

(1993),
1993 CanLII 4409 (MB CA)
,
83 C.C.C. (3d) 228
at 248
:

Courts should not be setting public policy
on the parameters of undercover operations.  The Crown's position,
with which we agree, is that the public would endorse rather than be shocked by
the efforts of the undercover agents in this case.

Hewak C.J.Q.B. rightly concluded that the
evidence in question was admissible.  We agree with his comments when
he said [at p. 253]:

In my view, on the facts of
this case, the undercover officers acted in a way consistent with the need to
investigate a very brutal crime.  Their actions were, without doubt,
different from the standard procedures, but they had to be, given the various
previous attempts made by them to investigate, bearing in mind the
circumstances of case, and lack of hard evidence.  They had
information that pointed in the direction they should follow, and in the
circumstances they devised and followed a plan that was appropriate to continue
with their investigation.

I find it difficult to
accept that a reasonable dispassionate person, aware of the difficulties in the
investigation of the case, would consider the undercover operation and use of
tricks by the officers, as being unfair or so unacceptable, indecent, and
outrageous, that the evidence that was derived from that operation, if admitted
as evidence in the trial of the accused, could bring the administration of
justice into disrepute.

[
59
]

If this Court finds that the objective of
police undercover investigations is a sufficiently important objective, it then
must consider
whether the
means employed by the police were reasonable and demonstrably justified.  This
court does so find and must, therefore, consider the proportionality test.

[
60
]

This involves a form of a proportionality test involving the above three
important components. To begin, the measures must be fair and not arbitrary,
carefully designed to achieve the objective in question and rationally
connected to that objective.  Second, the means should impair the right in question
as little as possible.  Lastly, there must be a proportionality between the
effects of the limiting measure and the objective ‑‑ the more
severe the deleterious effects of a measure, the more important the objective
must be.

[
61
]

The question, then, for this part of the analysis, is whether the
police investigative techniques, casting an undercover officer in the role of
an
Obeahman
, is rationally connected to the objective of curbing gun violence
in the community and apprehending offenders.

[
62
]

I find that the two are rationally connected.

[
63
]

Police officers must be granted the latitude necessary to
investigate crimes.  Particularly in the case of an undercover operation, the
details must be customized to the factual circumstances of the case.  In a case
where physical evidence is unavailable, obtaining admissions from suspects is
often the only means police have for furthering an investigation.

[
64
]

In this case, the plan developed by the police was highly nuanced
and focused.  The police did not enter into this investigation precipitously;
they gave thoughtful and careful consideration to the approach that would be
most effective in apprehending the suspected perpetrators of a violent crime.

[
65
]

In this Court’s ruling on the earlier
Garofoli
application,
R.
v. Welsh
,
Robinson and Pinnock
,
[2007] O.J. No. 2433
I found at
para. 47, that the police had demonstrated ample investigative necessity to
warrant the court issuing the second intercept authorization – that they had
met the test of showing their inability to present a viable case without the
further use of wiretaps.

[
66
]

The question at this point is whether the means employed by the
police constituted a minimal impairment on the Applicant’s religious freedom.

[
67
]

According to
Thomson
at para. 43, the minimal impairment
standard for governmental conduct is that the subject’s freedom be impaired as
little as possible given the government’s pressing and
substantial objective.  The police are not bound to find the least intrusive nor the best means
while impairing the individual’s rights.

[
68
]

Given the pressing and substantial objective of crime prevention, the
curtailment of Evol Robinson’s religious freedom during the course of his
meetings with the
Obeahman
constitutes a minimal impairment within the
meaning of s.1.

[
69
]

The police limited the scope of their investigation to a couple of
settings and to discrete interviews.  Beyond those minimal confines, the
Applicant’s freedom to practice his religious was not affected.

[
70
]

In keeping with Lamer C.J.’s adaptation of the
Oakes

proportionality test in
Dagenais v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp.
,
1994 CanLII 39 (SCC)
, [1994]
3 S.C.R. 835, at p. 889, the court must consider the proportionality
between the deleterious and the salutary effects of the police measures.

[
71
]

While the deleterious effects of such measures may at times include the
infringement of an individual’s
Charter
rights, those negative effects,
when measured against the salutary outcome to communities and society at large,
are disproportionately minimal.

[
72
]

In this case, the salutary effect of the police measure is the
furtherance of a criminal investigation into a gun-related death with the
objective of apprehending offenders and preventing further crimes of this
nature.

[
73
]

Where undercover police investigations prove successful, the salutary
effects resonate throughout the community.  Law-abiding citizens, fearful of
the random violence in their midst, are heartened by the prospect of living in
a less violent environment.

Conclusion

[
74
]

I, therefore, find that even if the undercover
police investigation did restrict Evol Robinson’s freedom of religion as
guaranteed under
s.2 (a)
of the
Charter
, the restrictions constitute a
reasonable limit demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society under

s.1
of the
Charter.

[
75
]

Hence, the police conduct did not violate the Applicant’s

Charter

right to freedom of religion.

The “Dirty Tricks”
Analysis

[
76
]

Having found the police investigation does not violate the Applicants’
Charter

right to freedom of religion, similarly the police conduct does not constitute
a “dirty trick” that would either shock the conscience of the community or
bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

The Alleged Section 15(1) Violation

[
77
]

The Applicants submit that the actions of the police constitute a
violation of their
s.15(1)

Charter

rights to equal protection and equal
benefit of the law without discrimination.  In particular, they argue that they
were discriminated against as a result of a police investigative method which
targeted them based solely upon their race, colour, national and ethnic origin,
and their religious and spiritual beliefs.  The statements obtained thereby
should be precluded pursuant to
sections 24(1)
and
(2)
of the C
harter
.

[
78
]

S.15 reads:

Every
individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal
protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in
particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

[
79
]

The analysis under s.15(1) proceeds in three
stages, with close regard to context.  At the first stage the claimant must
show that the law, program or activity imposed differential treatment between
the claimant and others with whom the claimant may fairly claim equality.  The
second stage requires the claimant to demonstrate that this differentiation is
based on one or more of the enumerated or analogous grounds. The third stage
requires the claimant to establish that the differentiation amounts to a form
of discrimination that has the effect of demeaning the claimant's human
dignity. The "dignity" aspect of the test is designed to weed out
trivial or other complaints that do not engage the purpose of the equality
provision:
Law v.
Canada
(Minister of Employment and
Immigration),

1999 CanLII 675 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 497;
Lovelace v. Ontario
, [2000]
1 S.C.R. 950,
2000 SCC 37
at a paras. 53-54.

[
80
]

In this case, the s.15(1) analysis need not proceed beyond the first
stage, as the Applicants have not shown that the investigative technique used
by the police imposed differential treatment on them in contrast to others with
whom the Applicants may fairly claim equality.

[
81
]

Criminality is not a protected analogous ground under s.15(1).  As a
suspect in a criminal investigation, the Applicants received the same treatment
any other suspects would have received under similar circumstances.  They were singled
out and targeted by the police not on the basis of their race, but on the basis
of their suspected involvement in a serious and violent offence.  They just happened
to be black, of Jamaican heritage and therefore possibly susceptible to the
Obeah

sting.  The police undercover tactics were not motivated by racism.  They were
motivated by a desire to solve a brutal killing.
Having
exhausted other avenues for obtaining evidence, the police engaged in a novel undercover
operation, customizing the setting, the approach and the techniques to the
particular facts of this case.
Even if in some
way the Applicant’s s.15(1) equality rights were infringed, for the same
reasons noted above, the investigative techniques employed constituted a
reasonable limit under
s.1
of the
Charter
.

Religious Privilege

[
82
]

The Applicants argue that the inculpatory communications they had
with the
Obeah
man
are a form of “religious communication” and
are, therefore, protected by the common law religious privilege.  In
R. v.
Gruenke,

1991 CanLII 40 (SCC)
, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 263 at paras.
33-34
. the Court discussed and
interpreted the criteria for protection of religious communication established
by Professor Wigmore in
Evidence in Trials at Common Law,
McNaughton
Revision, vol. 8. Boston:
Little, Brown & Co., 1961.  These  are as follows:

(1)

The communications must originate in a
confidence that they will not be disclosed.

(2)

This element of confidentiality must be
essential to the full and satisfactory maintenance of the relation between the
parties.

(3)

The relation must be one which in the opinion of
the community ought to be sedulously fostered.

(4)

The injury that would inure to the relation by
the disclosure of the communications must be greater than the benefit thereby
gained for the correct disposal of litigation.

[
83
]

In determining whether or not religious
privilege should apply to the communications in question, this Court is mindful
of the constitutional implications as well as the multicultural sensitivities
engaged in this case.  The Wigmore criteria will be informed both by the
Charter

guarantee of freedom of religion and by the general interpretative statement in

s.27
of the
Charter
.

[
84
]

Having previously determined under the
s.2(a) analysis that
Obeah
is  a constellation of beliefs meriting
Charter

protection of religious freedom, I find that the communications at issue warrant
the case-by-case analysis approach established in
Gruenke
.

[
85
]

To succeed in their application based on religious privilege, the
Applicants must prove all four of the Wigmore criteria on a balance of
probabilities.  In
R. v.
Medina
,
[1988] O.J. No. 2348
,

Archie
Campbell J. discussed the criteria and what must be proved respecting each
one.  He said :

It is not necessary to consider whether
the tests are disjunctive or conjunctive although I am inclined to the view
that they are conjunctive, that the accused must meet all four tests to meet the
privilege and the failure to meet any one of the four tests results in the
failure to establish the privilege.

[
86
]

In that case the Court was considering a claim for privilege
covering communications between a religious leader and an individual later
accused of murder, who was attempting to flee the jurisdiction.  Campbell
J. set out the following criteria for evaluating the confidentiality of the
communication:

(1)  Does the communication involve some aspect
of religious belief, worship or practice?

(2)     Is the religious aspect the dominant feature
or purpose of the communication?

(3)     Even if the religious aspect is not the
dominant purpose, how significant is it?  Would the communication
have been called into being without the religious aspect? Even if not the
causa
causans
, is the religious aspect the
causa sine qua non
of the
communication?

(4)     Is the religious aspect of the
communication sincere or is it colourable?  Did it amount to a good
faith manifestation of religious belief, worship or practice? If sincere and
asserted in good faith, the truth or falsity of the religious belief is
irrelevant.

[
87
]

The answers to these questions will not determine ultimate
admissibility, which must still be governed by the four-part Wigmore test. They
are intended only as a tool for the organization and analysis of the facts.

The First Test: Confidentiality

[
88
]

In order to meet this branch of the Wigmore
test, the Applicants must provide evidence that their communications with the
Obeah
man

were undertaken with an expectation that they would not be disclosed.  At paragraph
39 of
Gruenke,
the Court said “…it is absolutely crucial that the
communications originate with an expectation of confidentiality in order for
those communications to be qualify [sic] as “privileged” and to thereby be
excluded from evidence.  Without this expectation of confidentiality, the
raison
d
'être
of the
privilege is missing.”

[
89
]

Given the physical setting of the meetings, the atmosphere induced
by the
Obeahman
, and the gravity of the admissions made, the Applicants
would naturally have had some expectation of confidentiality.

[
90
]

This finding of an implicit expectation of confidentiality was endorsed
by the experts who testified to the confidentiality component of trust in
spiritual advisor/adherent relations.
[2]

The Second Test: Relationship

[
91
]

In
Medina
, Campbell J.

said:

The element of confidentiality may well be
essential to the full and satisfactory maintenance of a relation of pastoral
counselling between a pastor and his congregation. But the accused has not
established on a balance of probabilities that he went to the pastor for
pastoral counselling grounded in the word of God and the teachings of the
bible, rather than simply for assistance in fleeing the city and the country.”

[
92
]

This principle is applicable to the Applicants’ case. Pinnock’s and
Robinson’s motive in attending the
Obeah
sessions was not sincere
participation in a religious rite or service; rather, their purpose was to seek
protection from the evil spirit of the deceased Oraha and to cause harm to
those who sought to bring them to justice for allegedly committing a serious
crime.

[
93
]

The Applicants have not met the test in this second branch of the
Wigmore test.

The Third Test:  Community Interest

[
94
]

On this third branch of the Wigmore test, Campbell J. in
Medina
said:

The relation
must be one in the opinion of the community ought to be sedulously fostered. I
must take it as authoritatively determined by the guarantee of the fundamental
freedom of conscience and religion in s.2(b) [
sic
] of the
Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms
that the relation of pastoral counselling grounded in
the word of God and the teachings of the community ought to be sedulously
fostered.
There is, however, no community interest in protecting statements
made for the purpose of getting away after a crime.
Because the accused has
not established on a balance of probabilities Because the accused has not
established on a balance of probabilities any sufficient connection between the
statement and the relation of pastoral counselling, the third test has not been
met.

[
95
]

As one of the purposes of the Applicants’ communications with the
Obeah
man

was expressly to obstruct law enforcement officials and the judiciary from
prosecuting them, I find as did Campbell J. in
Medina

that the Applicants have failed the
community interest component of the Wigmore test.  They have not established on
a balance of probabilities a sufficient connection between their statements and
the relation of “pastoral counselling” or religious guidance.

The Fourth Test: Balancing the Values

[
96
]

In this final branch of the Wigmore test, the Court must balance the
benefits gained by disclosure of the Applicants’ communications against the
harm that would result to the “
Obeahman
-Adherent” relationship, should
the confidential communication be disclosed.

[
97
]

Once again, Campbell J. in
Medina

is instructive on this point:

On balance, I conclude on the particular
facts of this case that the clear harm to the effective prosecution of crime
and the proper administration of criminal justice, should this evidence be suppressed,
outweighs any potential harm to the relationship of pastoral counselling
between the pastor and his congregation. The accused has not met the fourth
test
.

[
98
]

Similarly, I find that the harm that would result should the
evidence be suppressed far outweighs the harm to the
Obeah
man
-Adherent
relationship.

[
99
]

As the Applicants have failed to meet at least three of the branches
of the Wigmore test, I find that their communications to the
Obeahman

fail the
Gruenke
test for religious privilege.

RESULT

[
100
]

Accordingly, the Application is dismissed.
